subQuestions.questionText: The revenue derived from the sale of one additional unit of a product is called … revenue.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D – marginal (2 marks)
Marginal revenue is the additional revenue earned from selling one extra unit of output.

subQuestions.questionText: The institution that investigates restrictive business practices is the Competition …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A – Commission (2 marks)
The Competition Commission is the South African body responsible for investigating restrictive business practices and anti-competitive conduct.

subQuestions.questionText: The cost that changes with the level of output is known as … cost.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B – variable (2 marks)
Variable costs change directly with the level of output produced (e.g. raw materials, wages of casual labour).

subQuestions.questionText: A market structure that is dominated by two producers is called ...
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D – duopoly (2 marks)
A duopoly is a market structure in which only two firms dominate the production and supply of a product.

subQuestions.questionText: A situation where prices rise so rapidly that people lose confidence in the value of money can be regarded as …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C – hyperinflation (2 marks)
Hyperinflation is an extremely rapid and out-of-control rise in prices, where money loses value so quickly that confidence in the currency collapses.

subQuestions.questionText: When tourists visit South African game farms, it is referred to as … tourism.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A – eco (2 marks)
Ecotourism involves visiting natural environments such as game farms, with a focus on conservation and the appreciation of wildlife.

subQuestions.questionText: The command and control approach that focuses on the environmental impact of pollution is called …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B – quality standards (2 marks)
Quality standards under the command and control approach focus on the environmental impact (quality of air, water, etc.) caused by pollution rather than the quantity emitted.

subQuestions.questionText: The process where trees are removed from the land and not replaced is known as …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C – deforestation (2 marks)
Deforestation is the permanent removal of trees from forested land without replanting, leading to environmental degradation.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: The period of production in which at least one of the factors of production is fixed.

Answer: Short run / Short term (1 mark)
In the short run, at least one factor of production (usually capital) is fixed, while others can be varied.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: A market in which illegal goods are bought and sold.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: Black market (1 mark)
A black market is an illegal market where transactions take place outside legal channels, often when official prices are controlled.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: The cost to society that is not included in the market price.

External costs are costs imposed on third parties or society that are not reflected in the market price of a good or service.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: Tourists from other countries who come to South Africa to visit places of interest.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: Type of inflation where the aggregate demand for goods and services exceeds the aggregate supply.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly discuss product differentiation and control over prices in monopolistic competition.
subQuestions.memoText:
PRODUCT DIFFERENTIATION (max 4 marks – award 2 marks per point, max 2 points):
• Different products are similar in that they satisfy the same consumer need but are not totally identical, e.g. variety of men's clothing.
• The difference may sometimes be completely imaginary, as in the case of medicines which may have different brand names but contain exactly the same basic ingredients.
• In some instances, it is merely the service of the seller that differentiates its product from others.
• The packaging of a product may make it different from other similar products, e.g. sugar and salt.

CONTROL OVER PRICES (max 4 marks – award 2 marks per point, max 2 points):
• Firms have little control over the price of a product due to the competitive nature of the market.
• They are price makers rather than price takers / price makers for their brand of products.
• Each seller can sell at its own price since a single price cannot be determined for differentiated products.
• A range of prices can be applied to different products depending on the size of the business.
• Bulk purchases by a business can result in lower prices for products.

[Allocate a maximum of 4 marks for mere listing of facts]
[Accept any other correct relevant response]

subQuestions.questionText: How would the implementation of maximum prices impact negatively on the economy?
subQuestions.memoText:

• The shortage in supply will result in the economy declining.
• Black markets often develop where producers may attempt to sell goods at higher prices.
• Producers of goods and services may leave the market as they are not making sufficient profits.
• Investors may withdraw their investment due to low return on their investment.
• A decline in economic growth and investment withdrawal will result in loss of jobs, leading to an increase in the level of unemployment.
• Maximum prices result in a decrease in supply which leads to an increase in prices of goods and services.

[Allocate a maximum of 2 marks for mere listing of facts]

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly discuss the effects of tourism on externalities and poverty.

• Rapid growth of tourism may lead to degradation of traditions and cultural values / environmental damage to sites and natural settings due to pollution and waste.
• Global tourism will grow due to increased population, improved living standards, increased free time and expansion of transportation systems.
• Tourism activities increase pressure on tourist sites.
• Tourism attracts revenue to the country, alleviates poverty, conserves cultural and natural assets, but needs to be carefully planned.
• Tourism can stimulate employment indirectly in tourism-related industries.

POVERTY (max 4 marks – award 2 marks per point, max 2 points):
• Tourism is widely recognised as a more effective mechanism to address poverty, especially in rural areas.
• Most prime tourism attractions are located in rural areas, which allow rural people to share in the benefits of tourism.
• Tourism provides an alternative to urbanisation, permitting people to continue to enjoy rural life whilst earning a living.
• Poor people are offered opportunities to link up with the mainstream tourism businesses by supplying goods and services.

subQuestions.questionText: How can the government promote a green economy in South Africa?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks each for any FOUR of the following points (max 8 marks):
• The government should make use of the Constitution as it allows it to create laws and methods to achieve a green economy.
• The government should enforce the National Environment Management (NEM) Act and other acts that are meant to deal with biodiversity, air quality and waste management to achieve a green economy.
• Taxes should be used to solve environmental challenges as they tend to be quite easy to implement and control.
• Revenue collected from taxes may be further used on measures such as environmental awareness to achieve a green economy.
• The implementation of the Industrial Policy Action Plan should be focused on achieving a green economy by using more advanced manufacturing techniques that are low in energy consumption and create green jobs.
• Clean energy and energy efficiency – expanding off-grid options in rural and urban areas, up-scaling solar water heater rollout.
• The government should promote the use of eco-friendly methods of energy production, such as wind, water and nuclear.
• Eco-friendly methods of energy production can be fast-tracked by allowing more independent power producers into the market to counter the pollution that is generated by Eskom.
• Incentives such as tax rebates can be provided to companies that produce environmentally friendly products.

[Allocate a maximum of 2 marks for mere listing of facts]
[Accept any other relevant and correct response]

subQuestions.questionText: With the aid of a correctly labelled graph, explain economic profit in a perfect market.
subQuestions.memoText:
GRAPH (max 4 marks):
• Labelling of axes (Cost/revenue and Quantity) = 1 mark
• Indication of profit maximisation point (e, where MC = MR) = 1 mark
• Correct drawing and labelling of revenue curves (D = AR = MR as a horizontal line at $P = R10$) = 1 mark
• Correct drawing and labelling of cost curves (MC and AC) = 1 mark
The graph should show: MC and AC curves, a horizontal D = AR = MR line at $P = R10$, profit maximisation point e at output $Q = 200$, and the rectangle 'Economic Profit' between $P = R10$ and $P_1 = R8$ (AC at e) up to Q = 200.

EXPLANATION (max 4 marks):
• The perfectly competitive firm maximises profit where marginal revenue (MR) and marginal cost (MC) are equal (point e).
• At point e, the firm will supply 200 units at the market price of R10.
• The average revenue is R10 and the average cost per unit is R8.
• Total economic profit will be $R400 = (R10 - R8) \times 200$.
• Total revenue is $R2\,000 = R10 \times 200$ and total cost is $R1\,600 = R8 \times 200$, so the firm makes economic profit of R400.
• Economic profit occurs in the short run.

[A maximum of 2 marks if the determination of economic profit is not explained]
[Accept any other correct relevant response]

subQuestions.questionText:
Examine oligopoly as a market structure in detail. (26 marks)
How can the government discourage firms from engaging in anti-competitive behaviour? (10 marks) [40]
subQuestions.memoText:
ESSAY MARK ALLOCATION:
• Introduction: max 2 marks
• Body – Main part: max 26 marks (max 8 marks for headings/examples)
• Body – Additional part: max 10 marks (max 2 marks for mere listing of facts)
• Conclusion: max 2 marks
Total: 40 marks

INTRODUCTION (max 2):
An oligopoly exists when a small number of large firms are able to influence the supply of a product or service in a market.
[Accept any other correct relevant introduction]

MAIN PART (max 26):
Number of sellers:
• There are few sellers dominating the market, which limits competition.

Nature of the product:
• Products may be homogeneous or differentiated.
• If the products are homogeneous, the market is regarded as pure oligopoly.
• When the products are differentiated, the market is regarded as differentiated oligopoly.

Market entry:
• Entry into an oligopolistic market is not easy due to the existence of barriers such as brand loyalty and economies of scale.
• Many oligopolistic industries have high set-up costs which also block entry.
• Advertising is very expensive, and firms that cannot afford to do so will lag behind the competition – this in itself is a barrier to entry.

Market information:
• Information is incomplete as consumers and producers do not have full information about prevailing market conditions.
• Lack of information may cause uncertainty and irrational decision-making in the market.

Control over the price:
• Producers have considerable control over the price of their product, but not as much as in a monopoly.
• Sometimes oligopolies may collude to influence prices in the market.

Demand curve:
• An oligopolist faces a kinked demand curve with two segments.
• The top segment is relatively elastic, and the bottom segment is relatively inelastic.
• [Allocate a maximum of 2 marks for a correctly drawn kinked demand curve]

Economic profit/loss:
• Oligopolistic firms can make economic profit in both the short run and long run.
• Barriers to entry make it possible for oligopolies to enjoy high profits.

Decision-making / Mutual dependence:
• The oligopolistic market is characterised by mutual dependency, where the actions of one firm will influence others.
• Interdependence leads to complex policy decision-making compared to other market structures.

Collusion:
• There is a high possibility of collusive practices in an oligopoly since there are few businesses.
• Oligopolistic businesses collude to reduce competition, earn higher profits and reduce uncertainty in the market.
• Collusion may be formal (cartels) or informal (price leadership).
• A cartel is an organisation of oligopolistic businesses that come into existence with the specific aim of forming a collective monopoly.
• Price leadership is the situation where the dominant firm fixes the price and the other firms accept it as the market price.

Non-price competition:
• Oligopolistic firms are reluctant to change prices because a price war will drive their prices down, eliminating profits.
• They make use of non-price measures to attract customers and increase their market share.
• An important aspect of non-price competition is to build brand loyalty, product recognition and product differentiation.

[Allocate a maximum of 8 marks for mere listing of headings and examples]
[Accept any other correct relevant response]

ADDITIONAL PART (max 10):
The government discourages firms/oligopolist firms from engaging in anti-competitive behaviour by:
• Granting licences to other businesses to compete against existing oligopolies.
• Imposing heavy fines on firms found guilty of anti-competitive practices/behaviour.
• Speeding up investigations on firms/businesses suspected of collusion/price fixing.
• Prohibiting mergers and takeovers by oligopolistic businesses with the aim of reducing competition.
• Implementing/introducing maximum prices on markets where there are possibilities of price fixing.
• Regulating unfair business practices, such as acquiring exclusive rights to resources, which may prevent new firms from entering the market.
[Allocate a maximum of 2 marks for mere listing of facts]
[Accept any other correct relevant response]

CONCLUSION (max 2):
Unlike perfect competitors, oligopolistic businesses fail to achieve both productive and allocative efficiency, as they do not produce at the lowest possible average cost and do not produce at the optimum output level.
[Accept any other correct relevant conclusion]

questions.title: Essay: Contemporary Economic Issues – Inflation (Section C)

subQuestions.questionText:
Discuss in detail the measures to combat inflation. (26 marks)
How do inflationary expectations affect the various role players in the economy? (10 marks) [40]
subQuestions.memoText:
ESSAY MARK ALLOCATION:
• Introduction: max 2 marks
• Body – Main part: max 26 marks (max 8 marks for headings/examples)
• Body – Additional part: max 10 marks (max 2 marks for mere listing of facts)
• Conclusion: max 2 marks
Total: 40 marks

INTRODUCTION (max 2):
Inflation refers to a sustained and significant increase in the general price level over a period of time, with a simultaneous decline in the buying power of money.

BODY – MAIN PART (max 26):

MONETARY POLICY MEASURES (taken by the South African Reserve Bank):
Interest rates:
• The SARB curbs inflation by increasing the repo rate, which makes it expensive to borrow money.
• Banks pass on the increased cost of borrowing (repo rate) to their clients by increasing the interest rate.
• High interest rates discourage consumers from taking unnecessary credit, discouraging consumer spending.
• A decrease in credit creation results in a reduction of money supply, thereby reducing demand-pull inflation.
• The increase in interest rates stabilises the value of the currency, which helps to reduce cost-push inflation through lower import costs.

Open market transactions:
• The SARB can directly decrease the supply of money by selling government securities in the open market.
• When banks buy these securities, money flows from banks to the SARB, which reduces money supply.
• Reduction in money supply will reduce aggregate demand, controlling demand-pull inflation.

Cash Reserve Requirements:
• Commercial banks are required to hold a certain minimum cash reserve with the central bank.
• An increase in the cash reserve requirement limits the amount of money that banks can give out as credit and helps to curb inflation.

Moral suasion:
• The SARB can persuade commercial banks to act in a responsible manner when granting credit under inflationary conditions.
• Moral suasion helps to reduce inflation because credit will be granted to fewer consumers.

FISCAL POLICY MEASURES (changes in taxation and government expenditure):
Government expenditure:
• The state can reduce expenditure by postponing some government projects such as roads, hospitals and schools.
• Aggregate demand will decrease, thereby reducing demand-pull inflation.
• The government may finance a budget deficit from the non-banking sector to limit inflation.

Taxation:
• Government can increase direct taxation, such as personal income tax, to decrease demand.
• An increase in indirect taxation (VAT) causes spending to decrease because goods become more expensive.
• The state can impose surcharges on imported goods, which will increase their prices and discourage consumer spending.
• A loan levy can be used to reduce the disposable income of consumers.
• The government may reduce taxes on savings or introduce tax-free savings accounts to encourage saving and reduce spending.

OTHER MEASURES:
• Increase productivity – improved education and training allow more people to be employed and ensure they are more productive.
• Price control – the government ensures that certain essential goods remain affordable by fixing their price.
• Wage policy – a wage policy should keep wage increases in line with the inflation rate.
• Stricter conditions for consumer credit – the National Credit Regulator may impose strict requirements on consumer credit, which will reduce aggregate demand.
• Import controls are relaxed – more imports may help to supplement local supply of goods and services, reducing inflation caused by product shortages.
• Floating exchange rate – prices are automatically adjusted to international conditions, which allow free operation of the price mechanism (real prices).
• Indexation – refers to a policy of linking prices of items such as wages, pensions and mortgage bond interest rates to price indices to eliminate the effects of inflation.

ADDITIONAL PART (max 10):
Various role players are affected by high inflation expectations in the following ways:
• Inflation expectations play a major role in the process that transmits expectations of price increases through to the actual increase in prices.
• Consumer spending may increase when consumers expect prices to increase in the near future, without market signals.
• More consumer goods and capital goods are bought before the price increase, thus increasing aggregate demand.
• Labour unions demand higher wages to protect the purchasing power of their members when they anticipate a rise in inflation.
• When wages increase, businesses raise their prices to compensate for the increase in labour costs, thereby fuelling inflation.
• When businesses expect inflation to rise, they tend to increase their prices in advance, which increases their profit margins.
• The SARB uses inflation expectations to adjust monetary policy instruments that control money supply.
